{  "passage_id": "DICKENS_GREAT_EXPECTATIONS_001",
  "condition": "simplify",
  "rewritten_text": "I hurried along as fast as I could, and just after crossing a ditch I knew was near the Battery, I climbed up the mound beyond it. There, I saw a man sitting in front of me. His back was to me, his arms were folded, and he was nodding forward, clearly very sleepy.

I thought he would be happier if I surprised him with breakfast, so I quietly walked up and tapped him on the shoulder. He jumped up instantly—but it wasn’t the same man! It was a different man.

Still, this man looked similar in many ways. He wore rough grey clothes, had an iron on his leg, was limping, had a hoarse voice, and was cold, just like the first man. The only difference was his face and the flat, wide-brimmed hat he wore. I saw all this in a flash, because I had only a moment to take it in. He cursed at me, swung at me with a weak, round blow that missed me and nearly knocked him down, and then he ran into the fog, stumbling twice before disappearing.

'It’s the young man!' I thought, my heart pounding as I realized who it was. I imagine I would have felt pain in my liver too, if I had known where it was.

I soon reached the Battery, and there was the right man—hugging himself and limping back and forth as if he had been doing nothing else all night—waiting for me. He was very cold, and I half expected to see him fall down and die from the cold. His eyes looked so hungry that when I gave him the file and he placed it on the grass, I thought for a moment he might try to eat it if it wasn’t for my bundle. This time, he didn’t turn me upside down to get what I had. Instead, he let me open the bundle and empty my pockets.

'What’s in the bottle, boy?' he asked.

'Brandy,' I said.

He was already shoving mincemeat into his mouth in a strange, hurried way, more like someone trying to hide something than someone eating. He stopped to take some of the liquor, but he was shaking so badly that he could barely hold the bottle’s neck between his teeth without biting it off.

'I think you’ve got the ague,' I said.

'I agree with you, boy,' he said.

'It’s bad around here,' I told him. 'You’ve been lying out on the meshes, and they’re terrible for causing chills. They’re rheumatic too.'

'I’ll eat my breakfast before they kill me,' he said. 'I’d do it even if I was going to be hanged on that gallows over there right after. I’ll beat the shivers, I bet you.'

He was eating mincemeat, meat bone, bread, cheese, and pork pie all at once. He kept looking around distrustfully at the fog around us and often stopped, even stopped chewing, to listen."

’Then, Herbert,’ I would reply, ’let’s look at our affairs.’
